Of the bottoms of the two empty jars here with me, one was broken that same year, and the other is still sitting on the top of the rack in the woodshed out back, untouched for twelve years. Whether the fire brand is there, whether it is freight-depot goods—at daybreak I will move a ladder and take it down for you to see.”
She gently closed the account book, pressed both hands on the cover, and after pressing there for a while, said in a low voice:
“I will not interrogate that person, nor am I in a hurry to speak up for Brother Zhou. I only want one thing made clear: who took those two jars of shaodaozi, and where they poured them. If they were poured on the goods—then whether my Brother Zhou went to put out the fire, or was tricked into delivering the jars, there must be an explanation.”
She raised her head, and her voice suddenly brightened, cutting away a layer of the heaviness pressing down on the room:
“Old Zhao! Don’t let the fire in the kitchen die down, dawn is almost here! A-Fu—are those three gentlemen on the communal bunk still snoring? If they are, good. Keep sitting there!”
Then she turned back and moved the small lamp a little closer between the two of them, illuminating the account book, the receipt, the bronze token, and the unopened package of twenty taels.
“The third entry. Go on. That medicinal materials shop Shen Guihe has in the East Market—are there two bluestone mortars standing at its entrance? If so, ten years ago I delivered goods inside for someone.”
She pinched the abacus bead between her fingers, looked at him, and waited for the next one.

Lu Wenfeng fingers the third abacus bead, but does not let it fall: “Yes. The stone mortar on the left is missing a corner, and the backyard medicine cellar leads straight to an underground river. If what you sent in ten years ago was not medicinal herbs, but an empty jar sealed with the fire mark of Qixia Ferry—then this third entry matches as well.”
He looks at her: “Don’t guess yet. What did you deliver back then, and who signed for it?”

Liu Sanniang gently placed the counting bead in her hand back into its groove—not letting it fall, and not allowing it to retreat.
“I don’t guess,” she said. “Accounts guessed out are muddled accounts. I have ledgers at this counter.”
She turned and lifted the counter board again. This time she pulled out the third volume from the top; on the cover was written “Renyin.” She did not open it right away, but first trimmed the lamp wick, then went down page by page—until, at a certain page, her hand stopped, for longer than it had stopped before.
“Ten years ago, third month, twenty-second day,” she read, her voice flat. “‘Transferred on behalf: twelve empty jars, warehouse fire marks on the shoulders of the jars, mud seals newly made; also thirty jin of dried bamboo shoots, two jars of fermented fish, sent to Deshan Medicinal Materials Shop in the East Market of Lin’an. Porterage four hundred wen, received. Not entered in accounts.’”
She pushed the ledger over, her fingernail pinning the next line.
“Deshan. That shop is the very one you mentioned—the two blue-stone mortars at the door, the left one missing a corner. What I delivered was listed as dried bamboo shoots and fermented fish; the jars went along with them. That year my shop had only been open two years, and I didn’t have much ready money. An old canal contact passed me a porterage job, and I took it. Twelve empty jars—I thought at the time: a medicine shop taking jars to hold medicinal wine, perfectly natural.”
Her throat moved once.
“I saw the fire marks on the jar shoulders too. I even found myself an excuse—if a warehouse burned down, and the jars scattered onto the river, whoever picked them up could use them. They weren’t worth anything.”
Her fingernail slid half an inch downward and stopped at the receipt entry.
Then her whole body went rigid.
It was not the character “Shen,” nor was it any private seal. It was a mark—a crooked “seven,” with a long horizontal stroke dragging below it, like a steelyard carrying a weight.
Liu Sanniang stared at the mark and said nothing for a long while. The lamp flame jumped twice in her eyes.
“...Han Qijin.” At last she spoke, her voice so low it was almost no human sound at all. “He couldn’t write his name. He drew this and called it the ‘seven-jin scale.’ At the incense table, he knelt on my right-hand side.”
Slowly she drew her hands back from the ledger and wiped them again and again on her apron, as if she could not wipe them clean.
“Master Lu, count the days. That fire was twelve years ago. This entry was ten years ago. Han Qijin died in a foreign place in the third year after the fire—nine years ago.” She raised her head; the whites of her eyes were filled with red veins. “In other words, these twelve empty jars of mine, carrying the fire mark of Qixia Ferry, were received in the East Market of Lin’an on behalf of Shen Guihe by a living man who ought to have been mourning the dead for two years, two years after the fire. One year after he signed, he died away from home. I never even saw his corpse; the one who brought word of his death was a traveling peddler.”
She suddenly let out a laugh, a laugh as if someone had seized her by the throat.
“A traveling peddler. The one in my courtyard tonight had new carrying ropes too.”
She braced both hands on the counter board. After holding herself there for a moment, her back straightened inch by inch.
“The third entry matches.” She reached out and pressed that counting bead down. With a crisp, clear “clack,” she said, “—but I’m marking it as ‘uncleared.’ Meng Shisan sank to the bottom of the river, and I believed it; Brother Zhou’s face, Gu Changting wouldn’t let me see, and I accepted that too; but this entry for Han Qijin—from now on, I won’t believe a single word of it. At daybreak I’ll send word out to investigate that funeral affair from nine years ago in that foreign place: who reported it, where he was buried, and whether there’s anyone in the grave.”
Only after she finished speaking did she seem suddenly to remember something. With one sweep she gathered the ledgers, receipts, and bronze token into her arms, rolled in the packet of twenty taels as well inside her apron, rose, walked to the foot of the counter, lifted the brick, stuffed everything back in as it was, pressed the brick down tight, and kicked two handfuls of broken firewood over it.
“Dawn’s almost here.” She patted the dirt from her hands, and her voice brightened all at once; she was the shopkeeper again. “The three gentlemen in the common bunk have to catch a boat at the chen hour, so the fermented fish needs heating first; I settled the account for the one at the east end last night, two qian and two; the peddler’s carrying pole is still in my courtyard—I’m not touching that pole. If the authorities come asking about it someday, I’ll say a guest left it behind, and not one word more.”
She grabbed a rag and wiped it across the counter. Halfway through, she stopped and turned back to look at him; the red veins in her eyes had not faded, yet her words were perfectly proper and composed:
“Master Lu, go upstairs and sleep for an hour. The Tian-zi room is yours. All three nights have been paid for, and I only changed the mat on the bed yesterday.”
After a pause, she flung the rag over her shoulder.
“I’ll call you at the chen hour. I’ve already marked the noodles as ‘paid’—extra broth, lots of scallions. Old Zhao is to use the first pot of broth, not the second. When you come down and finish eating, we’ll compare the fourth entry.”
She turned toward the stove. With her back to him, her voice dropped half a notch, as if she were speaking to herself:
“Brother Zhou, Meng Shisan, Han Qijin... I did not misread a single one of those three names tonight.”

Lu Wenfeng presses down on that account book: “Don’t put it away yet. Make a rubbing of this page, and hide the original account book elsewhere—the proof is easiest to lose before daybreak.”
He flicks down the fourth abacus bead: “In the escort-payment ledgers of Yongtai Firm over the past nine years, ‘seven-jin scale’ appears every year. Han Qijin isn’t dead; at the very least, this hand is still keeping accounts for Gu Changting. With a face check ahead, we won’t be sleeping; after we eat, we’ll go meet this dead man.”

Liu Sanniang glanced at the hand pressing down on the account book. She did not push it away; instead, she herself nudged the book another half inch toward him—as if handing off half of something too hot to hold.
“Take a rubbing.” She said only that one word, and had already turned toward the stove.
When she came back, she held three things: a sheet of thin cotton paper cut to size—the kind she normally used for writing the menu; a small dish of fine ash scraped from the stove pit; and half a lump of lard. She laid the cotton paper over that page, rubbed ash onto the pad of her finger, and pushed downward finger by finger—the shadows of the ink marks first showed through the paper, and then she took up a brush and traced along those shadows. She traced extremely slowly, stroke by stroke, exactly the same way she had copied those four names beneath the counter on that night twelve years ago.
“I trace characters slowly. Don’t rush me.” Her eyes did not leave the paper. “For that mark ‘seven-jin scale,’ I have to match the length of the horizontal stroke. In the future, when it’s compared against the pledged-funds ledger, even half a fraction off will let people say it’s forged.”
After she finished tracing, she blew it dry and spread a thin layer of lard across the back of the paper—like oiled paper, impervious to splashed water.
Then she picked up the original account book, went to the woodshed, moved over a ladder, climbed up, and took down from the top of the rack the empty jar that had been covered in dust for twelve years. She held the jar in her arms and first wiped its shoulder with her sleeve—beneath the dust, a firebrand mark emerged: Qixia Ferry Freight Depot.
She looked at that brand for a while before wrapping the account book in oiled cloth, stuffing it into the jar, grabbing the fresh clay by the stove, and pressing it on palmful by palmful, sealing it tight. Once it was sealed, she shoved it deep into the woodpile and covered it securely with old bamboo-shoot husks.
“The original account is in this jar.” She patted her hands, mud still sticking between her fingers. “The old rule on the canal—empty jar, fresh mud seal, not entered in the accounts. Twelve years ago I used this method to deliver things for Shen Henian; today I use it to press down on his life. Apart from me and Lao Zhao, no one knows which pile of firewood this jar is under.”
She folded the rubbing copy into quarters and tucked it into the inner shirt against her body; then she put the crane-patterned bronze token, Gu Changting’s receipt, and that packet of twenty taels all back together beneath the third brick at the foot of the counter.
“I carry the rubbing; the original account stays in the shop; the proof is pressed under the brick.” She counted each item out to him, as if quoting the prices of dishes. “Three places, separated. What you said was right—before daybreak is when proof is easiest to lose. My shop may have two bolts at night, but it isn’t made of iron.”
Straightening up, she suddenly drew in a breath, and her voice opened wide at once, so bright the whole wooden building seemed to shake:
“Lao Zhao—first pot of broth, two bowls of noodles! Plenty of broth, extra scallions. One bowl marked on the counter as ‘paid,’ the other under my own name; I’ll pay the ten wen! Afu! Get up and boil water. The three gentlemen in the common bunk have to catch a boat at the chen hour; heat the wine-lees fish first, slice the glutinous-rice lotus root and plate it—they’ll eat it on the road!”
Only after shouting did she turn back to look at him. The bloodshot streaks were still in her eyes, but her words came steadily:
“After we finish the noodles, I’ll go with you.”
She raised a hand to stop the sentence he was about to say:
“Hear me out. You still have one night left in the Tian-class room. I won’t refund the room money, and I’ll keep the room for you—so when you come back at night, you’ll have a place to rest. That’s the rule of my shop. Afu will watch the counter. The Di-class room is one qian, the common bunk twenty wen; he can quote the prices and take the money. I’ve already scolded him enough about rounding off the small change. Lao Zhao handles the stove; he’ll guard the jar by the back door. The shop won’t close.”
She untied her apron, folded it neatly, and pressed it onto the innermost stack of account books on the counter. Then from beneath the counter she felt out that old cowhide wrist guard—the one she had let him use last night—and now she put it back onto her own left forearm, fastening each clasp tight.
“I’m not bringing a knife.” She spread both empty hands for him to see; her palms were still stained with mud and ash. “I said these hands of mine would only hold a lamp tonight. I’ll bring abacus beads, the rubbing, and a mouth—Gu Changting has risen three ranks, Shen Guihe runs an apothecary; people like that aren’t afraid of knives. They’re afraid of accounts. In these twelve years behind this counter, what account have I ever failed to balance?”
She pressed that fourth abacus bead even more firmly with her finger.
“East Market in Lin’an, Deshan Medicinal Materials Shop, two bluestone mortars at the entrance, the left one missing a corner. Ten years ago I delivered twelve jars to that courtyard. I never went into the medicine cellar in the back courtyard—but if you say it connects directly to an underground river, then I know one more thing: this end of the underground river links to the reed marsh three li below Guangping Wharf. Nine years ago that stretch of marsh was a fish pond leased by the Yongtai Firm. I know that route. I escorted cargo through it.”
At this point she paused. The corner of her mouth slowly tugged into a faint smile—not the bright face of an innkeeper, but the smile of the woman escort from the ferry crossing back then, thin as a blade.
“Let’s go meet this dead man.” She said in a low voice, “If Han Qijin is still alive, I won’t touch him. I only want to ask him one question to his face: those two jars of Shaodaozi liquor that Brother Zhou got on credit—who told him to put them on the tab?”
From the stove came a splash—the noodles had gone into the pot. She turned to fetch the bowls, took two steps, then looked back again, her voice brightening once more:
“Master Lu—the first-pot broth. Eat it all. There’s no hot food for the twenty li on the road. I’ve marked this bowl as ‘paid’; you’re not allowed to leave a single mouthful.”

Lu Wenfeng picked up the noodle bowl, lowered his head, and took a bite. “The soup is good, and the account is clear. After we finish eating, we take the water route and don’t enter through the main gate of East Market—since Han Qijin kept accounts for Gu Changting for nine years, he may not be the only one meeting today.”
He paused. “You asked about those two jars of wine. I’ll watch his hand for you. People can lie; hands won’t.”

Liu Sanniang had not touched her own bowl of noodles. First she laid her chopsticks crosswise over the bowl, then turned and carried out two more empty jars from behind the firewood stack—this time they were clean, with no fire mark on the shoulders of the jars; they were the ones she used at home for pickling fermented fish.
“Hands don’t lie.” She repeated the sentence in a low voice, knocked the mouth of a jar against the table edge, and chipped off a ring of dried mud. “Hearing that makes my heart go cold—because I also remember a pair of hands.”
She held out her own right hand and bent her index finger.
“That finger of Han Qijin’s was once twisted off by a cable while unloading hemp sacks at the ferry. It was reattached crooked, so it juts outward. When he holds a bowl, pinches a scale weight, or draws that ‘Qijin scale,’ this is the finger that sticks out first.” She withdrew her hand and pressed it against her apron. “A face can be nourished back, a voice can be feigned, a name can be changed, but that finger cannot. Master Lu, you look at his hands, and I look too—you look at what he takes; I look at how he takes it.”
As she spoke, she moved one empty jar onto the counter, threaded straw rope through it twice, then picked up the fermented fish that had just come out of the steamer and poured it in together with the soup, sealing it with lotus leaves and pressing it down with mud. Into the other jar she stuffed thirty jin of dried bamboo shoots and sealed it tight.
“We take the water route and do not enter through the front gate—on that point, you’re right. But slipping into someone’s back courtyard with two empty hands would make us thieves.” She patted the jars, and in her eyes there suddenly lit up the gleam of someone who had calculated an account to its cleverest point. “Ten years ago, what I delivered to Deshan was under the heading ‘thirty jin of dried bamboo shoots, two jars of fermented fish.’ If the gatekeeper in that courtyard is still an old hand, once he smells this fermented odor, his hand will go open the back gate on its own—I’m not sneaking in; I am the delivery runner, coming to collect the four hundred wen delivery fee from the year before last. A debt collector standing in someone else’s courtyard is the least conspicuous thing under heaven.”
From beneath the counter she dragged out an old bamboo hat and a washed-pale short jacket, tossed them over her shoulder, then unfastened that string of copper keys and sorted through them one by one. The Tian-numbered room key with the greenish copper rust—she held it and glanced at it, then pushed it in front of him.
“You keep this one. The room costs four qian for three nights; I’ve taken the payment, I won’t refund it, and I’ll keep the room for you for one night—whatever hour you come back tonight, there will be hot water. This is the rule of my shop, and it has not been broken in twelve years.”
Then she slapped the remaining keys onto the counter board and called out:
“Ah Fu—come here! The counter is yours today. The Di-numbered room is one qian; a common bunk is twenty wen. Quote round numbers; not one wen may be shaved off! Say the Tian-numbered room is full; even if someone offers three qian, it is still full! If anyone asks about what happened in the shop last night—listen clearly: you don’t know, you didn’t see, there is no such person. If anyone wants to search the account books on my counter, say the shopkeeper took them away; if they want to enter the back courtyard, say half the firewood stack there has collapsed and it’s too filthy to stand in. Remember this: my shop stands on one word, ‘trust.’ If that word is broken, next year all of us will have to go carry shoulder poles for a living.”
She went toward the stove again, lowering her voice by half a notch:
“Old Zhao, guard the jar with the fire mark under the firewood. Whoever comes today to ask for firewood, buy firewood, or deliver firewood—we sell none of it. If I don’t come back, you wait until I do.”
Only after finishing her instructions did she pick up her own bowl of noodles. Standing by the counter, she shoveled it clean in two or three mouthfuls, drank even the broth to the last drop, and knocked the bottom of the bowl with a “da.”
“Ten wen.” From the money box she counted out ten copper coins and threw them back into the box one by one, each sound ringing clear. “My own account, I settle myself.”
Only then did she grab the two jars, one at each end, sling the straw rope over her shoulder, and carry them with remarkable steadiness—the shoulder that had not borne loads in twelve years, yet its bones remembered the position on their own. She pressed the bamboo hat down over her head, down to her brow bone.
“I’ll lead the water route.” She tilted her head toward the door. “Three li below the stone wharf, we turn into the reed marsh. In the marsh there’s a little channel used by water-chestnut pickers. We won’t take the main river, and we won’t pass the wharf’s likin checkpoint. The boatman is an old subordinate of mine from the canal transport days; he doesn’t recognize people, he recognizes jars—he only asks, ‘How many?’ I answer, ‘Two,’ and there’s no more talk. We go ashore at the open drying ground for medicinal herbs at the north end of the East Market, twenty paces from Deshan’s rear wall.”
She stopped on the threshold and looked back at him. The bloodshot streaks had not yet faded from her eyes, but they were no longer the eyes from last night that had been about to catch fire—they were a shopkeeper’s eyes, weighing jin and liang, judging the heat.
“One more thing: I’ll say it in advance.” She did not take the jars off her shoulders, but her back was ramrod straight. “I will not touch him. Today these hands of mine will only carry jars and flick abacus beads. If he is alive—I will ask him to his face who told him to put those two jars of shaodaozi liquor on credit; if he is willing to speak, I will put him on the boat too, alive, to keep him for settling accounts.”
After a pause, her voice dropped, so low that only the one chi of space by the door could hear it:
“But if he juts out that crooked finger and calls me ‘Sanniang’—Master Lu, keep watch over my own hands for me.”
She lifted her foot and crossed the threshold. The river wind lifted the edge of her bamboo hat, and the sun was just climbing up from the river’s surface in a layer of white light. Suddenly she raised her voice again and threw one last sentence back into the hall, bright and open, as though she were merely going out on an ordinary errand for goods:
“Ah Fu—leave a pot of soup for tonight! Master Lu and I will still want noodles when we come back; first batch, wide broth, extra scallions—two bowls! Put it all on the counter account!”
Only when she was walking down the stone steps did she add half a sentence, extremely softly, as though entering an account for herself:
“Twelve years. Today it’s time to settle it.”

Lu Wenfeng takes a jar and hoists it onto his shoulder, saying flatly, “Both bowls are on me. When we reach the medicine cellar, just collect the debt; if Han Qijin calls your name, look at his hand first, and don’t answer.”
He lowers his bamboo hat and walks toward the stone wharf: “The dead recognize old acquaintances easily; the living can die from recognizing the wrong person.”

Liu Sanniang followed three steps behind him. The jar on her shoulder pressed the straw rope into her flesh, yet she deliberately did not switch shoulders—if she switched shoulders, her steps would be thrown off. That had been the rule when escorting goods twelve years ago.
“Putting both bowls on your account won’t do.” She spoke from behind the brim of her bamboo hat, her voice lowered, yet still in the same tone she used at the counter. “I already threw the ten wen for my bowl back into the cashbox, counted it in front of Ah Fu—ten sounds. If you pay it again, there will be ten extra wen in my accounts. An excess is harder to settle than a shortfall. Your bowl is recorded as ‘paid’; my bowl is recorded as ‘own meal.’ Each entry belongs where it belongs. Neither of us owes the other.”
After saying this, she laughed first herself, a somewhat hoarse laugh. “...I know what you mean. But this is all I have left in this life, Master Lu. Accounts must be clear, doors must be bolted, and lamps must be left burning. Don’t change that for me.”
The fog at Shibu Wharf had not yet dispersed. A narrow black-awning boat lay against the reed roots, and at the bow crouched a man wearing a felt hat, not raising his head.
She set the jar on the gangplank and said only, “Two.”
“...Aboard.” The boatman also said only two words. With a push of the oar, the boat left the wharf.
Once they entered the reed marsh, the waterway narrowed. Reed leaves scraped against the awning overhead in a rustling sheet. She pushed her bamboo hat back, revealing half her face, and only then took out from her robe the oil-soaked rubbing, spread it on her knees for a glance, then quickly folded it back up and tucked it into her inner garment close to her body.
“I remembered what you said.” She suddenly spoke, her eyes on the water. “‘The dead are easy to recognize by old memories; mistaking the living can cost lives.’”
Her fingers slowly curled on her knees, one by one.
“I couldn’t lie down last night, so I kept thinking about that. I hope he’s alive—I hope it so much it frightens me. Master Lu, think about it: if Han Qijin is alive, and these nine years he has been at the counter of Yongtai Firm, recording accounts stroke by stroke for Gu Changting, then he wasn’t tricked away by someone. He was sitting behind someone else’s counter. Those two jars of shaodaozi wine of Brother Zhou’s were put on credit by him for someone else; when this hand of mine passed the jars out, he was standing at the door of my shop.”
She raised her hand, looked at her own palm, then clenched it into a fist.
“For these twelve years, every Qingming I’ve burned paper offerings for him. I was burning them for a living man keeping accounts for someone else.”
The reed leaves flashed, and light leaked in to fall across her face. She swallowed that breath down, and her gaze settled, like the beam of a steelyard coming to rest level.
“So I will not answer.” She said it very clearly. “If he calls ‘Sanniang,’ I won’t turn my head. I will only watch how that crooked finger on his right hand grips things—if it is him, I’ll collect my four hundred wen in porterage fees, not yielding a single wen. I’ll recite to him every entry of the carrying accounts from the year before last, from ten years ago, one stroke at a time, until his hand shakes. If his hand shakes, I won’t need to ask the rest. He will speak himself.”
She paused, then added one sentence, like adding a small remainder to an account:
“If he doesn’t shake... then it really isn’t him, and I’ll carry the jars home and make noodles. That is fine too. That is also a clear account.”
The boat scraped against the bank and stopped. At the northern end of the East Market, the open ground for drying medicine was spread under the sun with aged tangerine peel and baical skullcap; the smell was so sharp it made the nose bitter. She jumped ashore first, took the jar from his shoulder, steadied both of them together, then lowered the brim of her bamboo hat and walked toward the back wall of Deshan—twenty steps, a water well, a small black-lacquered door.
When she reached the door, she did not knock the ring. She raised her hand and rapped on the door panel with her knuckles: three long, two short, with a half-breath pause in the middle.
The old rhythm used in the canal trade for collecting porterage fees.
Inside the door there was a breath of silence, then the sound of slippers scuffing underfoot. The door opened a crack, revealing half an old face. The person looked at the jars on her shoulder, then at her bamboo hat.
The first sentence that person spoke was not to ask who she was.
“...How many jars?”
The sweat on the back of Liu Sanniang’s neck chilled at once. She heard her own voice steady to an astonishing degree, as steady as if she were quoting dish prices:
“Two. One jar of fermented fish, thirty jin of dried bamboo shoots. Four hundred wen in porterage fees from the year before last—I’ve come to collect.”
She shifted half a step sideways inward, propping the crack of the door open, while her eyes, from beneath the bamboo hat, fixed straight on the hand holding the doorframe—
Then, extremely softly, just enough for the one person behind her to hear:
“Master Lu. The one opening the door is using the canal trade’s way of asking. ...In this courtyard, Han Qijin is not the only one who recognizes the jars.”

Lu Wenfeng supports the bottom of the jar, his gaze sweeping over that person’s right hand: “Don’t identify the person first; identify the route first. We’ll count the four hundred wen after you enter—may I trouble the ‘seven-jin scale’ who signed for it to come out?”

Liu Sanniang did not wait for the gatekeeper to let her in. First she set down the jar of pickled fish on her shoulder with a “thud” just inside the threshold—this was the old rule of porters: once the goods crossed the threshold, the account was considered to have come to the door, and no one could drive it out.
“Please make half a step of room, sir, the jar is heavy.” She spoke with a smile, her face full of the air of oil and salt, but she had already slipped sideways through that half step. Her bamboo hat pressed down over her brow, and her eyes looked upward from beneath its brim. “Please don’t mind my nagging—when I deliver goods, I have to report the account face to face. If I report it wrong, I’ll be scolded when I go back.”
She unloaded the second jar as well, straightened her back, and casually took a small abacus-bead case from inside her clothes. She set it on the stone platform of the well in the courtyard, her fingers flicking it with a clattering “huala” sound, and reported in a clear voice:
“Renyin year, third month, twenty-second day, transferred by Liu Sanniang: twelve empty jars, thirty jin of dried bamboo shoots, two urns of pickled fish, sent to Deshan Medicinal Materials Shop in the East Market of Lin’an. Porterage fee, four hundred wen. The receipt was signed by ‘Seven-Jin Scale’—a fingerprint mark, not a signature; I recorded it here as a mark. This entry: the goods were received, but the money has been pressed on your counter for ten years, not a single wen paid.”
She raised her head, her smile not diminishing in the slightest:
“Ten years. By the rules of my counter, porterage fees gain one fen for every month overdue. I have not added a single fen. Principal and interest together, I ask only for the principal—four hundred wen, exact. These two jars today are still under the old item name; I will not ask for new porterage either. Settle the old account first. Once it is settled, I leave. If it is not settled, I will sit here on this well platform. I brought dry rations.”
Her report was watertight, but her eyes never left the hand braced on the doorframe for even a moment.
The left hand was bracing the door. All the fingers were there, the fingernails thick, and at the web between thumb and forefinger was an old rope-gouge mark—the hand of someone who had hauled towlines on the canal. But the right hand hung at his side from beginning to end, hidden inside the sleeve, not moving at all.
In her heart, one bead of that abacus quietly fell: what old gatekeeper would not reach out to take goods? If he did not take them, it meant he refused to show his right hand.
She also swept the courtyard with one glance: on the east side, scutellaria and dried tangerine peel were being aired, the medicinal smell pungent; from the cracks around the row of medicine cabinets on the west side, a chill leaked out, and on the ground a wet trace seeped from the bottom of the cabinets all the way to the foot of the wall—water was running underground, its sound extremely faint, a “gulu” rising through the brick seams. Her nose twitched, and beneath the medicinal smell filling the courtyard she caught a very faint stench—the stench of a riverbed, not of fish.
The underground river was right beneath there. She fixed this place firmly in her mind: if they had to retreat, go that way; if something happened, that was also the other side’s escape route.
“As for the person who signed for it—” She closed the abacus-bead case, her voice brightening, bright enough for the entire courtyard to hear. “I am here to collect a debt, not to identify a person. Whoever made the mark should come out and answer for it; if he does not come out, then this account has no owner. Surely your esteemed firm would not have a woman who runs an inn go back and tell her workers: Deshan’s account—no one acknowledges it.”
At this point, she suddenly lowered her voice, until only a thread remained, yet every word was bitten off solidly:
“Go report this: Liu Sanniang of Banhuchun, here for the porterage on those twelve jars from ten years ago, has come under the original item name to collect four hundred wen. If he does not remember me—then tell him three words.”
She paused. Her heart was pounding like thunder, and her fingers pinched a white mark into the abacus-bead case.
“‘Not entered in the accounts.’”
The left hand that the gatekeeper had braced on the doorframe suddenly tightened at the knuckles.
Liu Sanniang saw it perfectly clearly, but the smile on her face became even more amiable. She stepped back half a pace, leaving the empty space beside the well platform open, and even courteously straightened the mouths of the two jars for them.
“I will wait here.” She pushed her bamboo hat up by a finger’s width, revealing a pair of perfectly calm eyes. “I can draw water myself; no need to trouble anyone.”
As she turned to draw water, with her back to him, she scattered half a sentence very softly, only enough for the person behind her to hear:
“Master Lu—his right hand has been hidden in his sleeve the whole time. The one we are asking about—perhaps there is no need to ‘invite’ him; he is already in this courtyard, watching us himself.”
She flung the well rope, and the bucket fell into the well with a “splash,” loud enough for the whole courtyard to hear.
But in her heart she repeated only one sentence: Han Qijin, if you are alive—then you are behind some window in this courtyard, and you have heard the three words “not entered in the accounts.” Whether you come out or not, I am going to settle this account today.

Lu Wenfeng takes out a string of copper coins and deliberately tosses it to the right side of the porter: “Four hundred wen can be settled on the spot—please do me the favor of catching it steady with your right hand. Han Qijin, that crooked finger of yours has been hidden for nine years; aren’t you tired?”

Liu Sanniang did not look at that string of copper cash.
She stood by the well platform, her back to the door, still clutching the well rope in her hand—she listened.
With a clatter, the copper coins scattered onto the ground. She heard it clearly: not the muffled sound of being caught, but the crisp sound of them rolling all over the floor. The porter had not used his right hand; he had swept his left arm across to block them, and missed.
The copper coins bounced and rolled across the brick floor, one, two, three. One kept rolling, rolling all the way under the row of medicine cabinets at the west end, where it struck a cabinet leg with a “ding” and stopped.
Then the courtyard fell silent, with only the smell of medicine left.
Silent for one breath—
From the small door left ajar at the very bottom of the medicine cabinet, a hand reached out to feel for that copper coin.
Liu Sanniang had her back turned and did not look around. She only turned half her face to the side; beneath the bamboo hat, those eyes followed the reflection in the pool of water on the well platform and looked over.
On the water’s surface that hand wavered: three fingers pressed against the bricks, the index finger not pressing down, but sticking outward—crooked like the beam of a scale that had been broken and then reattached askew.
Her chest gave a buzzing thud, yet her whole body loosened instead, so much so that she nearly lost her grip on the well rope. Twelve years of Qingming paper offerings, twelve years of the right-hand side of the incense table, nine years of Yongtai Firm’s pawn ledgers—all of it had come to rest on this one finger.
She slowly wound the well rope back around the post, one loop, two loops, winding it with perfect steadiness. Then she turned around, without taking off her bamboo hat, without taking a step, standing where she was, and once more held that little abacus-bead box in her hands.
She did not shout “Han Qijin.” She did not answer to that name, nor did she call that name—she simply opened her voice, spreading it into that dish-calling tone the whole hall could hear, bright and clear, as if she were behind the counter of Banhuchun Inn:
“Honored guest—don’t pick up those copper coins. Even if you do, they won’t count as settling the bill.”
Her fingertip flicked an abacus bead. “Tak.”
“Four hundred cash for porterage. I won’t take ready money today.” She paused, then reported downward in an even voice, “I want to exchange it for an account.”
“On the twenty-second day of the third month in the Renyin year, twelve empty jars, the jar shoulders bearing the fire brand of Qixia Ferry Freight Depot, signed for with the mark ‘Qijin Scale’—for this entry, I wrote three characters myself: not entered in the accounts. I was the one who wrote them, and I was also the one who handed over the jars. For ten years I treated it as business. Only today do I understand whose hand I handed them to.”
She flicked another bead.
“On the seventeenth day of the seventh month in the Gengzi year. Zhou Dalang bought two jars of Shaodaozi liquor on credit at Banhuchun Inn, totaling one hundred and eighty cash, recorded under my account, to be offset when the goods arrived.”
Her voice suddenly dropped, so low that it pressed another layer over the medicinal air filling the courtyard, yet every word struck the bricks:
“He didn’t drink Shaodaozi. He drank warmed Nü’erhong, and even complained that I warmed it too slowly.”
The abacus bead stopped between her fingers. She did not flick it down.
“I did not come today to identify a person. I came to reconcile accounts. I am setting these two entries here; whoever acknowledges them, answer for them.” She raised her eyes and looked straight beneath that row of medicine cabinets. “Those two jars of Shaodaozi—who told him to buy them on credit? I have waited twelve years for this one sentence. Answer it, and I will write off these four hundred cash. From then on, no one owes anyone.”
She took a deep breath, set the abacus-bead box onto the well platform, and spread both hands open, palms upward, letting the whole courtyard see.
“I have no knife in my hands,” she said. “And I will not touch you. I was a shopkeeper for twelve years, and I have stood on one word alone: trust. When a person enters my door, I do not sell him out; today, standing inside your door, I will not deceive you either. I have a boat on the river, its cabin floor laid with straw, no lamp lit. That is not a road to death; that is a road to life—you get on it, live, and speak slowly.”
At this point, she suddenly smiled, her eyes reddening, yet her voice was as steady as a scale beam settling level:
“Qijin. That finger of yours was mangled hauling cables at the ferry; I treated it for you. At the incense table, you knelt to my right; when you knocked your third kowtow crooked, I was the one who set you straight.”
“If you still recognize the sound of these abacus beads of mine—then come out on your own.”
She said no more, and did not move.
Only tilting her head slightly, so softly that only the person beside her could hear:
“Master Lu, watch that wet mark on the west side. If he runs, he will take the underground dark river—once he moves, seal the opening with the pole. Don’t hurt him. I want him alive.”
She paused, then added half a sentence, as if adding the final odd sum at the counter:
“...Tonight’s two bowls of noodles, I still remember them as ‘paid.’”

Lu Wenfeng steps sideways to seal off the wet trace on the west side, his hand still not on his sword: “Han Qijin, what Sanniang recognizes is old affection; what I recognize is accounts. Come out and answer for those two jars of wine; hide one breath longer, and I’ll take it that everyone in this courtyard doesn’t want to live to settle accounts.”

Liu Sanniang heard the little door beneath the medicine cabinet creak open with a “zhi”; the wooden hinge was short of oil, crying out like a groan.
She did not step forward, nor did she speak.
What emerged first was that hand. Five fingers braced against the bricks, the index finger jutting outward, trembling from the strain—the man had crawled out. He crawled to the side of the well platform before propping himself on the cabinet leg and rising bit by bit.
He was thinner. He wore a pharmacy assistant’s short blue-cloth jacket, the cuffs stained with baical skullcap powder. There was little color in his face, and an old scar had appeared over his left brow bone. She stared at that face for three breaths, still leaving herself a thin margin in her heart: not him, not him—but when the man lifted his head, the way his eyelids drooped downward was exactly the same as the young fellow who had knocked his head askew before the incense table twelve years ago.
“…Sanniang.”
She did not answer.
She heard a “ge” inside her heart, like an abacus bead being flicked all the way down. She slowly wiped both hands on her apron—she had not brought an apron, so she wiped at empty air. Then she lifted the abacus-bead box, flicked down that one bead: “da.”
The sound was so crisp that the medicinal smell in the whole courtyard seemed to tremble.
“You recognize that sound.” She finally spoke. Her voice was hoarse, but its pitch was still the pitch she used at the counter, bright and open, refusing to let herself cave in. “Then let’s settle the account. Four hundred wen—I’m writing it off. I don’t want this debt.”
With a push of her finger, the abacus beads returned to zero.
“I only want those two jars of shaodaozi liquor.”
Han Qijin’s knees went weak, and he knelt among the scattered copper coins covering the ground. His right hand pressed against the bricks; that jutting finger shook so badly it could not hold steady. His throat bobbed twice, and the voice that squeezed out was broken like sand:
“…That liquor wasn’t what Brother Zhou wanted. I put it on credit. I put it on credit using his name.”
The abacus-bead box in Liu Sanniang’s hands tightened.
“Go on.”
“Gu Changting’s men gave me three taels of silver and told me to put two jars of shaodaozi liquor on credit, put it on Banhuchun’s account—on your counter, in Brother Zhou’s name, and have it entered in the account book.” He raised his head; his eyes were empty. “I carried the jars to the back of the inn and handed them to someone, then I left. The next night, the fire started. Sanniang, I didn’t know… I truly didn’t know what they wanted those two jars of liquor for—until I stood outside the fireground and heard Gu Changting read that document, ‘careless kitchen fire.’ Only then did I understand what that entry of mine was for.”
Liu Sanniang stood without moving.
In her mind, that “Gengzi” account book opened by itself: Seventh month, seventeenth day, Zhou Dalang, two jars of shaodaozi liquor on credit, one hundred and eighty wen, entered under Liu San’s account. Her own handwriting. Her own ink.
—That was not a credit entry. It was a piece of witness testimony. Written twelve years ago, written in her ledger, proving that someone in the warehouse at Qixia Ferry had bought two jars of fierce liquor to start a fire, and that the man’s name was Zhou Dalang.
She had safeguarded this evidence for someone for twelve years, and every Qingming she had even burned paper offerings for him.
A fishy taste surged up in her throat. She gritted her teeth and swallowed it back down, wiping the corner of her mouth with the back of her hand. Only after wiping did she realize she was laughing—laughing so hard her cheeks hurt.
“…So the rule in my shop,” she heard herself say, her voice so low it seemed to drift, “is not to sell strong liquor to drunkards. I kept it for twelve years. It turns out the very first one who sold the wrong liquor was me.”
The courtyard was silent for one breath. Beneath the damp streak on the western side, there came an extremely faint “gu”—water pushing up, then falling back.
Her whole body abruptly woke.
“Master Lu, seal it!” With that cry flung out, she had already lunged two steps forward. She did not touch Han Qijin; instead she bent first, tore away the lotus-leaf seal on the jar of fermented fish, splashing fishy soup over half the brick floor, then grabbed the mouth of the jar and turned it on its side. “Qijin, crawl in—I'm not coaxing you. Someone in this courtyard wants your mouth shut, and there’s a boat moving at the other end of the hidden river!”
Her hands and feet moved so quickly that she herself had no time to understand it; the bones that had escorted cargo twelve years ago made the decision for her. Straw rope looped around, the jar mouth turned downward and covered the man’s head and face—the old canal method for hiding people through checkpoints. Stifling, but one could survive three li of water.
“Gatekeeper!” She turned and roared, making all the dried tangerine peel in the courtyard tremble. “Pick up every last copper coin from that string of yours for me! I have written off the four hundred wen; I, Liu Sanniang, have written it off in person—today Deshan does not owe Banhuchun Inn a single wen, and Banhuchun Inn will never again take this route of yours! Go report to your employer Shen Guihe: I’m taking the jar back today, and I’m taking the man back too. If he wants to settle accounts, tell him to come to the Banhuchun Inn by the river and settle them—there has not been one muddled entry on my counter in twelve years!”
After saying this, she shouldered up that jar, gritted her teeth, and straightened. It was so heavy that her vision went black, but her feet remained steady.
She tilted her head and left only one sentence for the person beside her, so soft that only one person could hear it:
“…He isn’t the inside traitor. He is the pen someone else used.”
After a pause, the thing in her eyes that had burned for twelve years finally fell, settling into frost on a knife edge.
“The one truly holding the pen is sitting in the county seat.”
“Master Lu—clear the way. Get him onto the boat, alive. I owe him a question, and he owes me a mouth; this account is not yet balanced.”

Lu Wenfeng kicks over a medicine rack, blocking the entrance to the underground river, his hand on his sword hilt: “Put the jars down and let him walk on his own. Han Qijin, if you want to board the boat alive, then talk as you walk—those two jars of wine, who did you hand them to?”
He turns sideways to stand in front of Liu Sanniang: “Sanniang, stay close to me. Don’t look back.”

Liu Sanniang put that jar down—not throwing it, but crouching and slowly setting it steady, with the mouth facing upward, afraid it would break.
Then she pulled out the length of straw rope at her waist, grabbed Han Qijin’s right wrist, wound the rope end around it twice, and tied the dead knot on the back of his own hand—his feet were not bound, and one finger’s width of slack was left at the wrist.
“Walk yourself,” she said in a low voice, her eyes not on his face, only on that jutting finger trembling under the rope. “I’ll lead you. If you run, I drag you; if you fall, I haul you up. For twelve years I failed to hold on to Brother Zhou. Today I’m holding on to you.”
One hand holding the rope, the other pushing at the man’s lower back, she shoved him until he stumbled forward; she herself shifted half a step to the side and followed steadily behind Lu Wenfeng’s shoulder.
“Stay close. Don’t look back.” She repeated it once, as if carving the words into her own bones. “—I won’t look back anymore either.”
The three of them rushed toward the small back-wall door over copper coins scattered all across the ground. A whole section of medicine racks had toppled, dried tangerine peel and scutellaria spilling until bitter medicinal fumes surged through the courtyard. The gurgling sound of water from the dark-river mouth at the west end was pressed down by the wooden racks, muffled underneath, like something holding its breath in the cracks between the bricks. The porter clung to the base of the wall, his face white as paper. She flung her final words at him brightly, still in that counter-side dish-calling tone, each word striking the ground:
“I am writing off the four hundred cash in front of you! Deshan does not owe Banhuchun Inn a single coin today—remember this clearly: I, Liu Sanniang, am writing off the account myself! If your master wants the man or wants the jars, tell him to come to Banhuchun Inn by the river and settle it with me!”
Twenty steps out through the little door, the herb-drying yard lay ahead, the sun dazzling white. She shook the rope and dragged the man toward the little creek by the reed marsh, gasping after three steps, but not stopping even as she gasped.
“Speak,” she said through clenched teeth. “The question Master Lu asked you. Those two jars of liquor—who did you hand them to? Speak as you walk. Make it clear and I’ll send you onto the boat. There’s straw laid inside, no lamp lit, and you’ll live.”
Han Qijin was yanked into a stagger, his throat wheezing, the words spurting out in broken pieces:
“I... I carried them to the firewood door behind the depot. Someone took them! Wearing the depot’s livery, with a fire brand on the cuff... I didn’t see his face, he had his hat brim pressed low... I only saw the hand he used to take the jars—”
“What about the hand?” Her voice sank at once.
“Left hand! The left hand was wrapped in cloth... that hand wrapped in cloth, the little finger... gone. When he took the jars, the jar shoulder scraped it, and I saw under the cloth that half of it was missing—”
Liu Sanniang’s steps suddenly stopped.
The sun in the yard hammered down on her bamboo hat, yet she felt ice along the back of her neck. Twelve years ago, three days before the fire broke out, that cloth-wrapped hand that came to the ferry in the middle of the night to buy liquor on credit; Brother Zhou had said, “That hand isn’t right. Remember it.” She had remembered for twelve years, remembering only that piece of cloth.
Last night. Her own back alley. That slab of bluestone.
“...He is on my boat.” She heard herself say it, hoarse almost beyond words. “Master Lu, the one we pinned down last night—that was the man who received the jars twelve years ago. He isn’t a new blade used by Shen Guihe—he is an entry from the old account, used for twelve years and still not thrown away.”
She suddenly laughed once, laughed until her eyes burned, while the rope in her hand was clenched deathly tight.
“No wonder they want to kill you.” She lowered her head to look at Han Qijin. “You are the pen, and he is the hand. Put pen and hand together, and Gu Changting’s claim of ‘kitchen fire caused by negligence’ can no longer stand.”
She raised her head, yanked the rope forward, and her voice brightened again, bright enough to startle a flock of waterbirds from the reed marsh:
“Go! The little creek is right under the reed roots. The boatman recognizes jars, not people—I’ll call out ‘two,’ then add ‘one more person’! Qijin, you lie in the bottom of the cabin, and don’t shut your mouth. Talk all the way to the stone wharf!”
After running a dozen steps, she called out again, as if adding the final odd sum to this long account:
“Master Lu—we’re not going back to the East Market. We’re going back to the inn! Both ends are in my hands: the hand on the boat, this pen on the rope, the stamped note with Gu Changting’s private seal under the cabinet-foot brick, and the empty jar with the fire brand in the woodpile. Put the four things on one table, and this account will balance!”
Panting, her bamboo hat slipping to the back of her head and ignored, she turned back and cast one hard look at the back wall of that medicine firm—after all, she still looked back, just once.
“...Tonight, two bowls of noodles, extra broth and extra scallions.” She wiped her face, her voice dropping. “Tonight I want three bowls. The extra one, I’ll set at the corner of the counter—Brother Zhou’s place. No one has sat there for twelve years.”

Lu Wenfeng cuts the pursuing trip-rope and shields the two of them as they duck into the reed marsh: “The three bowls are lit, but we won’t go back to the shop yet—if Shen Guihe comes after us, we can’t bring disaster to Afu and the others. Get on the boat first and switch waterways; we’ll go pick up Night Harrier. Let this pen identify that hand face to face.”
He glances at Han Qijin: “Keep talking. That ‘kitchen fire caused by negligence’ from Gu Changting—who delivered it into your hands?”

Liu Sanniang plunged headfirst into the reeds. Reed leaves scraped fiery lines across her face. She freed one hand and pushed Han Qijin’s head down. “Stay low! Show even the top of your head and you’re a target.”
When they ran to the small channel, that narrow black-awning boat was still pressed against the reed roots. She tossed the rope end onto the deck, her voice forced extremely low:
“Two—plus one person. Change waterways, don’t go back to the stone wharf. Three li downstream, inside the reed marsh, that fishpond—the one Yongtai leased nine years ago. At the end of the pond there’s a half-collapsed watch shed for the fish. If your boat didn’t go far last night, it will be moored there.”
The man in the felt hat only gave an “Mm.” With a push of the oar, the boat slid into the shadows of the reeds.
Only then did she sit down heavily on the gunwale, panting so hard her chest rose and fell. But first she took from inside her clothes the rubbing that had been smeared with lard, glanced at it, then tucked it back against her body—the oil paper was not wet, and she let out half a breath of relief.
“We’re not going back to the shop. You were right.” She wiped the water from her face, her voice hoarse. “But I have to send a word over, or that child A’Fu will still be guarding the pot of soup for me after dark.”
She reached under the cabin planks and dragged out an empty jar—one boatmen kept year-round, with no mark on its shoulder. She tore off a corner of a menu card, wrote three characters with a charcoal stub, added two dots outside the circle, stuffed it into the jar, grabbed a handful of pond mud to seal it shut, and pushed it into the water. The jar spun as it followed the current toward the stone wharf.
“Empty jar, fresh mud seal, not entered in the accounts.” Watching the jar drift away, she gave a self-mocking laugh. “I’ve used this method for twelve years. Ten years ago, this was how I passed twelve jars to Shen Henian too.”
At that name, she suddenly turned her head and stared hard at the person in the bottom of the cabin:
“Qijin. Answer what Master Lu asked you. That paper saying ‘accidental kitchen fire’—who delivered it into your hands?”
Han Qijin was curled up on the straw. The crooked finger on his right hand trembled so badly it could not press down on the cabin plank, and his throat rasped:
“…It was the accountant at the depot. Mr. Shen—Shen Henian. He came to me with the document and said the dates from above had to match, told me to ‘fill in’ that debt for wine on credit—the date, the ink color, the signature, each and every thing had to line up. If even one stroke was off, someone would die… Sanniang, I was only nineteen then. He said someone would die, and I truly thought it meant I was going to get someone killed…”
Liu Sanniang slowly straightened.
The reed leaves rustled overhead, and sunlight fell in strips through the gaps onto her face. She was silent for a long time before speaking, her voice astonishingly level:
“Shen Henian. Shen Guihe.”
She extended two fingers and brought them together on her knee, as if joining two abacus beads into one.
“The same hand, with a changed name, went from being the accountant at Qixia Ferry to sitting as the proprietor of Deshan in Lin’an East Market. Twelve years ago he delivered documents; ten years ago he received jars; last night he set the Night Harrier to killing the brush.”
She suddenly raised her head. The redness in her eyes burned bright, yet instead she smiled—a very cold, very steady smile, the kind she only wore behind the counter when she had balanced a dead debt.
“Master Lu, I acknowledge this account.” She spread both hands for him to see. “These hands of mine have passed jars, written ‘not entered in the accounts,’ and put down those one hundred and eighty wen in the ledger. I won’t push it away. For twelve years I’ve eaten rice from muddled accounts—from today on, I will balance it myself.”
She wound that length of straw rope around the back of her hand once more and clenched it tight.
“When we reach the end of the pond, first let this brush meet that hand. Qijin, listen clearly: you recognize his hand, and he recognizes your signature. Once the two of you face each other and match them, that paper of Gu Changting’s saying ‘accidental kitchen fire’ becomes nothing but waste paper.”
After a pause, she raised a hand and pressed the bamboo hat that had slipped to the back of her head back down, all the way to her brow bone.
“The three bowls of noodles remain as ordered.” She said in a low voice, “When this matter is settled, we go back to the shop. The first pot of soup—that bowl I owe the corner of the counter, twelve years overdue, can finally be set out tonight.”

Lu Wenfeng looked at the ripples behind the reed marsh and lowered his voice: “Shen Henian is Shen Guihe. Mark that down for now; without evidence, don’t enter it as a final debt.”
He looked toward Han Qijin: “On that document, was Gu Changting’s private seal stamped first, or did Shen Henian stamp it in front of you?”

Liu Sanniang first pushed the abacus bead in her hand upward, back half a notch, not letting it fall.
“Right. No dead account.” She answered in a hoarse voice. “That is the counter’s proper duty—I nearly flicked it into a dead account just now. Shen Henian and Shen Guihe being the same person is my ‘suspicion,’ not my ‘account.’ Record it on the side, and wait for evidence.”
After speaking, she shifted herself to the bottom of the cabin and crouched down, one hand braced against the planks. Her face was almost up against Han Qijin’s as she lowered her voice extremely low, so low that only the rustle of reed leaves could cover it:
“Qijin, listen carefully. What Master Lu is asking about is not some major matter, but one very small thing—the more detailed your answer, the better. When that document was laid out right under your eyes: was that little seal already on the paper, or did Shen Henian dip it in seal paste and press it down in front of you?”
Han Qijin’s eyes darted wildly for a while, then suddenly froze, as if someone had yanked him back into that counting room twelve years ago.
“…It was already on the paper.” A dry laugh came from his throat, a laugh that frightened even himself. “The seal was printed on it, and the writing was blank. Sanniang, I remember clearly—he pushed the document to me and told me to fill in ‘the seventeenth day of the seventh month’ according to the date he dictated. The ink had to be old, not new. After I filled it in, my hand shook, and the ink bled a little. He cursed me, then drew another sheet from his sleeve—exactly the same, also sealed, also blank underneath.”
Liu Sanniang slowly stood up.
The boat brushed along the reed roots, and streaks of sunlight swept across her face overhead. She stood there, motionless, hearing only the “buzzing” in her own chest, so loud her ears began to swell.
“Blank seal.” She spat out the two words, extremely softly.
“Master Lu.” She turned around. Her voice was still low, yet steady as a steelyard settling level. “Before I opened the inn, I escorted official cargo on the grain transport routes. I understand this. For official documents, the contents are first written out clearly, then inspected by the presiding official before the seal is applied. Applying the seal first and filling in the words afterward—that is called a ‘blank seal,’ and it is a grave crime. Gu Changting was not covering up a fire for someone—he was handing stacks and stacks of blank documents with seals already affixed to Shen Henian, letting him fill in whatever dates he wanted.”
She extended one hand, her fingers tapping stroke by stroke in the empty air, as if she were flicking abacus beads.
“One burned down the freight warehouse, one sank Meng Shisan, one buried Han Qijin in a foreign place, and one sent me twenty taels of pension silver. In twelve years, just among the lives that came out of that stack of papers, I can count four.”
Suddenly she turned her head, her eyes pinning themselves to Han Qijin’s face:
“What about the second sheet? The one he drew out and didn’t use—where did it go?”
“…He took it back into his sleeve.” Han Qijin trembled as he spoke. “Sanniang, he never throws paper away. That kind of man has to cancel an account for a single wen three times over—that sort of paper, he wouldn’t burn it. He’d have to keep it to tally the count.”
Liu Sanniang slowly smiled.
“Then it is still there,” she said. “Shen Guihe’s Deshan—medicine sold in the front, a hidden river connected to the back courtyard. The medicine house’s claim tickets, the pledge ledgers—there must be some place that water can’t reach where they’re kept. Master Lu, I won’t enter this as a dead account. I’ll enter it as ‘to be retrieved.’”
She pressed that abacus bead downward by half a bit, not to the bottom, and stopped it there.
There was not even a “click.”
At that moment, the boatman in the felt hat gave the faintest “hiss” from the bow. The reed marsh suddenly opened out, the water surface brightened, and at the end of the pond stood a fish-watching shed with half its side collapsed, tilted there askew. In the dark shadow beneath the shed, an unlit black-awning boat was moored, with an empty jar hanging from its stern—the oar was wrapped in cloth.
Liu Sanniang drew in a deep breath, pressed the bamboo hat down to her brow bone, and wrapped the straw rope around the back of her hand one more turn.
“We’re here,” she said in a low voice. “Master Lu, you watch his hands; I’ll watch his mark. Qijin, get up—no kneeling. You’ve knelt for twelve years. This time, stand and identify him.”
She lifted her head and glanced at the sun, then added one sentence, like reporting an account that had to be recorded clearly:
“Once we have questioned him clearly in the shed, we go back to the inn. Three bowls of noodles, broth from the first pot—and the bowl at the corner of the counter, I will set it out tonight no matter what.”

Lu Wenfeng raises a hand to stop Han Qijin: “First identify the hand from behind the awning. Don’t let him see you, and especially don’t call his name first.”
He says in a low voice toward the unlit boat, “Boatman, have the man from last night extend his right hand. Qijin, just say whether you recognize it—if you do, then tell how he received the jars twelve years ago.”

When Liu Sanniang heard the words “right hand,” her fingers tightened on the grass rope—so tight her nails dug into her own palm.
She did not speak.
But in her heart there was a soft “click”: Master Lu, you are testing him. What Qijin said was the left hand, the cloth-wrapped left hand, the little finger half a joint short. Yet you deliberately asked about the right hand—if he follows your lead and answers “I recognize it,” then everything he has said about these twelve years was taught to him by someone else; if he is willing to contradict you, then this pen is real.
She swallowed that breath, not even casting a sideways glance toward Lu Wenfeng. She merely reached back, tore off her bamboo hat, held it in front of Han Qijin’s face, then pinched up the edge of the tarpaulin and, with her finger, propped open a slit one finger wide.
“Not a sound.” She pressed close to his ear, not daring even to breathe too heavily. “No calling names, no questions. Look through this slit—look at the hand, nowhere else. If you recognize it, say ‘I recognize it’; if you don’t, say ‘it’s not.’ Half a word more and I’ll cover your mouth.”
There was a rustling inside the unlit boat, the sound of straw. Someone pushed a hand out from under the awning.
The sun was just falling across the pond, and the dazzling white reflection struck that hand: across the back of it lay an old mark from being strangled by a mooring rope, the nails were thick and yellowed, and all five fingers were intact.
Behind the tarpaulin, Han Qijin made a “guh” sound in his throat.
“…Not this one.”
Liu Sanniang closed her eyes for a moment.
“It was the left hand.” Han Qijin’s voice trembled until it almost broke apart, yet each sentence was truer than the last. “The left hand was wrapped in cloth, white cloth, gone dirty. He used that hand to support the bottom of the jar—the freight-house firebrand on the shoulder of the jar, I had deliberately turned it inward, afraid someone would see it. When he took it, he scooped upward with that cloth-wrapped hand, and the shoulder of the jar pressed right against the base of his little finger. Under the cloth, half of it was missing. I saw it. In this whole life of mine, I saw only that one glance.”
“Boatman.” Liu Sanniang spoke, her voice hoarse, her tone as flat as if she were behind the counter announcing a small dish of food. “Trouble you—change to the left hand. Unwrap the cloth.”
There was movement under the awning again. The cloth-wrapped hand shifted out, the cloth loosening coil by coil, revealing a little finger cut off at the root—the break was old, the bone had not set properly, and it had grown into a crooked scarred knob.
Liu Sanniang stood at the side of the boat and did not speak for a very long time.
The reed leaves rustled. Three days before the fire twelve years ago, the cloth-wrapped hand that had come to the ferry landing at midnight to buy wine on credit; Brother Zhou setting down his wine bowl and saying, “That hand isn’t right, remember it”—she had remembered it for twelve years, remembered it into a strip of white cloth.
She slowly lifted the abacus-bead box and flicked down one bead.
“Click.”
“This entry goes into the dead account,” she said. “It wasn’t my suspicion; it was the pen and the hand being matched face to face—Qijin identified the hand through the awning, first contradicting the right hand, then recognizing the left hand’s little finger. That is called evidence. Master Lu, that question you asked just now nailed this account solid for me.”
She turned, snatched back the bamboo hat from in front of Han Qijin’s face, and pressed it back onto her own head.
“Boatman, bring the two boats together, half a zhang apart front to back. No lamps, no going near the dock. Keep these two under watch together: the pen in the rear cabin, the hand in the front cabin, one layer of awning between them—they are not allowed to see each other, and neither is allowed to speak. Don’t tell me where we end up; I won’t ask. I only want one sentence: at daybreak, they’re still breathing.”
When she had finished speaking, she crouched down, dragged another empty jar out from under the deck planks, tore off the last corner of the menu paper, wrote a few strokes with a charcoal stub, sealed it shut with a slap of mud, and pushed it into the water.
“Send this one back to Old Zhao.” She watched the jar spin. “Tell him to move the jar with the firebrand under the firewood stack into the cellar overnight, and then tell Old Sun, who sells water chestnuts at the mouth of the lane, to sit by my back door for the night—if Shen Guihe wants to come to Banhuchun Inn to check the accounts, let him come; the front door will be open. In twelve years, there hasn’t been a single muddled entry on my counter. But if he dares touch the rear courtyard—Afu only knows how to smash beans; someone has to help me hold that door down.”
She looked up at the sun’s shadow, then glanced again toward the depths of the reeds at the tip of the pond. The spark in her eyes sank back down, burning steadily.
“There are two things left to retrieve: Gu Changting’s second sheet of blank-stamped paper is still in Shen Guihe’s sleeve; and that night twelve years ago at the firewood gate behind the warehouse, after this hand took the jar, who did it pass it to?” Her knuckles tapped twice on the abacus-bead box. “I’ll mark these two entries as ‘pending retrieval,’ not as dead accounts.”
Then she patted the mud from her knees, stood up, and her voice suddenly brightened by a notch, so bright that another flock of waterbirds startled up from the pond:
“Back to the shop. Three bowls of noodles, broth from the first pot, extra broth and plenty of scallions—Master Lu, your bowl is marked ‘paid’; my bowl, ten wen for my own meal; the bowl in the corner by the counter…”
She paused, pushing the bamboo hat up by one finger’s width.
“The bowl in the corner by the counter, I’ll mark as ‘offered.’ After twelve years, Brother Zhou can finally sit down and eat something hot.”

Lu Wenfeng withdrew his gaze and said coolly, “Leave the character ‘feng’ for now. Put brush to paper only after the real accounts are settled. For the moment, we won’t return to the inn, and we won’t let Shen Guihe trace the boat route.”
He said toward the unlit boat, “Question him from across the awning—after he received the jar twelve years ago, which warehouse did he take the wine into, and whom did he hand it to?”

Liu Sanniang clamped down on the half-sentence she had been about to say and forced it back down—so hard it hurt her throat.
She suddenly remembered: last night in the rear courtyard, with one knee pinning that man’s back, she had put her mouth close to his ear and murmured a promise: “Double at the counter afterward.” That man had heard her voice. With only one layer of awning between them, if she so much as uttered two words, he would know who had pinned him down, whose boat this was, and which riverside inn this waterway led to.
She raised a hand, laid one finger across her lips, and shook her head at Lu Wenfeng. Then she crouched down, fished out that bit of charcoal, and wrote on the cabin planks—fast and large, each stroke like she was quoting prices on a menu:
“He has heard my voice. I won’t speak. Don’t say his name either, and don’t mention Banhuchun.”
When she finished, she looked up, waited for him to read it clearly, then added another line beside it:
“Let the boatman ask. I’ll write; he reads.”
The felt-hatted man leaned over. Without even lifting his eyelids, he took those words in. Liu Sanniang dipped the charcoal again and wrote line after line on the plank, the veins rising on the back of her hand as she wrote:
“Ask him: the one brought in at the west end of the warehouse—what number storeroom was it?”
“Ask him: on that warehouse ledger, was it recorded as ‘empty,’ or was cargo recorded there?”
“Ask him: the person who received the jar—what did others call him?—Don’t say the name. Make him say it himself.”
“Tell him: the pen is already in the next cabin; the pledge was that he took the jar with his own hands. If he is one sentence late, this whole account will fall on his head.”
“Then tell him: twenty taels, sealed as before, the sum promised to him last night—if he explains clearly, he gets the full amount.”
She flung the charcoal onto the cabin planks, withdrew behind the awning herself, pressed her back against the reed roots, and clenched both hands tightly around her knees without making a sound.
The boatman read the words out sentence by sentence, evenly, as if counting hemp sacks.
Inside the awning, there was silence for a long time. Water gurgled against the bottom of the boat.
Then the man spoke, his voice hoarse as if it had been soaked in water:
“...The third room at the west end.”
A chill ran over the back of Liu Sanniang’s neck.
“The ledger said it was an empty warehouse.” The man gasped for breath. “It wasn’t empty inside. It was piled up to the beams, covered with reed mats. I put the jar at the doorway, and a hand reached out from inside the door to take it—that time I didn’t go in.”
The boatman read the next line from the plank: “The person who received the jar—what did others call him?”
Inside the awning, there was another pause.
“Someone inside the warehouse shouted through the mat—” The man’s voice sank, so low it could barely be heard. “What he shouted was, ‘Master Ma, catch.’”
Liu Sanniang stayed pressed against the reed roots, not moving at all.
Master Ma.
Yongtai Firm at Guangping Wharf—twelve years ago it had still been called Yongtong, and the man in charge of the boats had the surname Ma. Last night behind the counter, she had recited that line, and when she did, she had only taken it as an old bit of news mentioned in passing.
She slowly raised her hand, brought over the abacus-bead box, and set her finger on that bead, but did not press it down.
After three breaths, she pushed the bead back upward by half a space.
Then she picked up the charcoal and wrote two lines on the cabin planks, for Lu Wenfeng alone to see:
“Don’t enter it as a dead account. Mark it ‘pending retrieval’—we need the warehouse ledger. If the warehouse ledger of the Qixia Ferry Freight Depot wasn’t burned, then after the fire it should have been sealed and stored by the authorities; after twelve years, the sealed register must be sitting in some storeroom somewhere. The ledger says West Third Warehouse was ‘empty,’ but the warehouse was piled to the beams—once this entry matches, Gu Changting’s ‘accidental kitchen fire’ becomes the crime he signed with his own hand.”
“Second item pending retrieval: in Yongtai Firm’s pledge-payment ledger, entries beginning with the character ‘Ma,’ over nine years. Qijin’s ‘seven-jin scale’ is there every year; let’s see whether this ‘Master Ma’ is there too.”
When she finished writing, she looked up. Her lips moved, but no sound came out. She only flicked her fingers in the air—as if moving abacus beads.
She wrote another line, slowly, each stroke pressed down with great weight:
“There is one more account, my own. Last night I promised him double. The twenty taels under the counter leg were the relief silver the authorities gave Brother Zhou. I originally said I would keep it to put up a grave stele. Today I used it to buy a mouth—I admit that, I don’t deny it. I’ll save up separately for the stele.”
The charcoal paused on the plank. At last, she gently pressed that bead down half a fraction, without a sound.
Then she stood, pulled off her bamboo hat and fanned the sweat on her face twice. Only then did she lean close to Lu Wenfeng’s ear, her voice so low it was only a thread:
“We won’t go back to the shop—I’ll listen to you. Go another li and a half inward through the reed marsh; at the end of the water-chestnut pond there are three thatched huts. Back then, they were a stopping place for escorting night cargo on the grain route. They recognized jars, not people. Behind the huts are two waterways, one leading into the reed marsh and one to the sluice gate. Put the paper in one room, the hand in another, and I’ll sit in the middle one.”
She pressed the bamboo hat back onto her head, down to her brow bones. The fire in her eyes burned with extraordinary steadiness.
“I won’t write the character ‘feng’ yet,” she said. “You’re right—the account isn’t settled, so I’m not fit to write it. But I won’t let Old Zhao’s pot rest; keep the broth hanging. When those two papers and that ledger are set on my counter, then I’ll write that entry.”
After a pause, she added another sentence, as if entering the day’s small balance:
“Three bowls. I remember.”

Lu Wenfeng wiped away the charcoal words on the cabin planks: “Don’t pay the double amount yet; his mouth hasn’t finished speaking. Go to the thatched hut. Pen and handprint separately.”
He spoke toward the inside of the awning: “That ‘Master Ma’—his full name, appearance, and what he now manages at Yongtai Company. And the goods covered with reed mats in West Third Warehouse—what are they?”

Liu Sanniang’s hands had already moved before her mind did—she tore a strip of white cloth from the lower hem of her inner shirt, spread it over her knees, dipped the charcoal stub in saliva, and wrote in large, urgent characters:
“Full name. What year did he start managing Yongtai Firm? Any marks on his face?”
“Under the mats in West No. 3 Warehouse—what goods were they? Make him say the name of the goods; he is not allowed to say ‘goods.’”
The boatman took the strip of cloth and read it aloud, reading in a flat voice, as though tallying sacks of hemp.
Inside the awning, it was quiet for a very long time, so long that Liu Sanniang could hear her own back teeth chattering.
“…Ma Deshun.” The man finally spoke, his voice scraping. “On the road they call him Ma Jiu. The left eyebrow is missing a section, scorched by fire—scorched that night twelve years ago. Two years after the fire, he went to Yongtong Firm; now Yongtai Firm’s goods inspections across the pond and the paperwork for pledged payments all pass through his hands.”
The boatman read the second item.
Inside the awning, there was a pause of one breath. Then the man spat out one word:
“Salt.”
The strip of white cloth on Liu Sanniang’s knees tore with a “chi”—she had clenched it apart herself.
“Official-permit salt,” the man continued. “Covered with reed mats, piled up to the beams. On the ledger it was written as ‘empty.’”
Liu Sanniang slowly stood up.
She stood in the shadows of the reeds, motionless, the trace of blood in her face draining away inch by inch.
Then she crouched back down and wrote on the cloth with the charcoal stub, writing extremely slowly, each stroke pressed so hard it tore the fabric:
“Master Lu. The fermented fish on my counter has been curing for twelve years; I handled the salt myself—I understand salt.”
“Salt is not afraid of fire. After the fire passes, salt turns into blocks, turns into brine, seeps into the soil. For years afterward, no grass will grow on that land, and after rain, white alkali will rise to the surface.”
She raised her head. Something in her eyes shone so fiercely it was frightening, yet she smiled once, very faintly.
“Master Lu, I went to the fire ground. I went on the fifth day after the fire; I wanted to see Brother Zhou’s face—Gu Changting wouldn’t let me. But I saw that patch of ground: it was white, patch after patch. At the time, I took it for ash.”
She wiped the back of her hand across her mouth and wrote again:
“The fire was not to dispose of goods. Salt cannot be disposed of by fire. The fire was to dispose of the ledger—the salt had been moved out already, leaving only an empty shell in the warehouse, and the ledger had already recorded it as ‘empty.’ Once the fire was set, the ledger burned, and the shortfall was balanced out. The two jars of shaodaozi liquor were to make the fire look like an accident at the stove.”
The charcoal stub stopped.
“A whole warehouse of official-permit salt. This isn’t smuggling; this is turning government salt into private accounts—what Gu Changting wanted was not to cover up a fire, but to erase a ledger.”
She folded the cloth strip, tucked it close against her body together with that rubbing, and pressed her hand against her chest, very hard.
“No double payment—I’ll listen to you.” At last she spoke in a low voice, pressed down beneath the rustling of the reed leaves, audible only to the person beside her. “His mouth hasn’t finished talking; the money doesn’t go into the till. But on my side, I have to add one entry marked ‘pending retrieval’: that patch of ground at Qixia Ferry. Twelve years have passed—whether grass has grown back, whether white alkali rises after rain—this entry doesn’t require asking anyone, doesn’t require begging for a ledger. I’ll take an iron spade myself, dig three chi of earth, boil a dipper of water, and know after one taste.”
She reached out and held the abacus-bead box, pressing that bead downward by half a fraction. It made no sound.
