“There is also one entry I don’t dare set down.” Her voice suddenly went hoarse. “What Brother Zhou was checking at the warehouse during those three days. He didn’t drink shaodaozi, and he wasn’t there to fight the fire either—he was a cargo escort. He knew how to inspect warehouses, how to count packages, how to lift mats.”
She closed her eyes.
“If he lifted those reed mats—then he wasn’t burned to death by the fire.”
A gap opened in the reeds. Ahead, at the tip of the pond, three thatched huts leaned into the water; behind the huts were two waterways, one leading into the reed marsh, one to the sluice gate. She pressed the bamboo hat down to her brow bone, her voice lowered and steady again, issuing instructions one by one as if settling guests for the night behind the counter:
“Bring the boats together. Put the hand in the east hut, the pen in the west hut; I’ll sit in the middle—neither side sees the other, no voices pass between them. Leave the waterway behind the huts that leads to the sluice gate open; lay the boat across there, and don’t put away the oar. Boatman guards the boat. No lamps all night.”
“Dry rations given separately, one portion each, and water separately too. If anyone calls out for water, I’ll deliver it myself—no third person is allowed near those two huts.”
“Send another jar back to the shop: tell Old Zhao to keep the broth simmering and not let it stop; tell Afu to open the doors tomorrow morning and sell noodles as usual, and say the Tian rooms are full; if Shen Guihe comes to check the accounts, keep the front door open and let him look at the account books—in twelve years, there hasn’t been a single muddled entry on my counter.”
She straightened, turning her head to look back at the dazzling white light on the water behind them.
“I won’t write down the character ‘offered.’” she said. “When that warehouse ledger, that sheet of blank-stamped paper, and those three chi of soil are all in hand, I’ll go back to my own counter and write it there.”
After a pause, she pressed the bamboo hat lower by another finger’s width.
“I still remember the three bowls of noodles. If they can’t be eaten tonight, they go on tomorrow’s account—I never round off my accounts.”

Lu Wenfeng first staggered the two boats and moored them steadily, then said calmly: “Salt-alkali can prove there was salt in the warehouse, but it can’t prove who emptied it. Record it first for later investigation.”
Through the canopy he asked again: “After Ma Deshun received the wine, who lit the fire? Did Zhou Dalang enter West Third Warehouse that night or not—what you saw with your own eyes, say it sentence by sentence.”

Liu Sanniang did not go into the middle room. First she crouched in the water under the eaves and washed her hands—washed them twice, scrubbing the pond mud, charcoal ash, and rotten-fish stink out from between her fingers. She herself did not know why she had to wash her hands this one time first. Only after washing did she lift the grass curtain and go in, sit down on the broken stool in the center, her back squarely facing the awning door of the room at the east end.
She took the torn piece of white cloth from her robe, spread it over her knees, and moistened the charcoal stub between her teeth.
Her hand was shaking. She watched that hand shake, endured it for three breaths, then used her left hand to press down on her right wrist—the way she had done when writing cargo slips in those years—before writing stroke by stroke, the characters large, heavy, the strokes pressing through the weave of the cloth:
“Ask him: after he set the jar at the warehouse door, when did he leave, and which road did he take.”
“Ask him: before he left, how many people were standing at the warehouse door, and how many lamps.”
“Ask him: those lamps—were they the depot’s signal lamps, or lanterns brought by the people themselves.”
At this point she stopped, the charcoal stub pausing on the cloth and pressing out a black hollow.
She raised her eyes and looked at the sheen of water outside the grass curtain. Her throat felt as if it were stuffed with a lump of dried bamboo shoot husk.
Then she wrote the next line:
“Ask him—on that night, was there a cargo escort in a blue cloth long gown, with a copper tally tube hanging at his waist, carrying a lantern and holding a small booklet, going toward West Warehouse Three.”
“Do not mention any name. Let him say for himself what that man looked like and what he was holding.”
She handed out the strip of cloth. The boatman took it and read from it, reading in a flat tone, as if taking inventory of hemp sacks.
Inside the awning, there was a long silence.
“...I set down the jar and left. Went back the same way, through the firewood gate behind the depot, then out along the foot of the wall.” The man’s voice seeped out from under the mat. “There were two lamps at the door. One was hanging under the warehouse eaves, the depot’s signal lamp. The other was being carried, carried by someone.”
Liu Sanniang’s two hands slowly clenched on her knees.
“The one carrying the lantern—” The man took a breath. “A long gown, blue. Something at his waist was clinking, copper. He also had a booklet tucked in his hand, thin, rolled up.”
“He was standing outside the warehouse door, talking to someone inside. When I left, I heard him say one thing—”
The thatched room was so quiet that only the pond water could be heard slapping against the wooden posts.
“He said: ‘I’m going to lift the mat.’”
Liu Sanniang’s whole body suddenly doubled over.
She shoved her fist into her own mouth and bit down, biting until her mouth was full of the taste of charcoal ash and rust. A muffled “hoh” sounded in her throat, and she swallowed it back down hard. Tears smashed onto the white cloth on her knees; one drop spread the character for “lift” into a blur.
She bit her own hand until that surge of force had passed, then took her fist down. A ring of teeth marks on the back of her hand was so deep it had gone white.
Then she picked up the charcoal stub.
Her hand was no longer shaking.
On the cloth she wrote—wrote extremely slowly, stroke by stroke, in the same manner as when she had traced that “seven-jin scale” last night:
“Enter one settled dead account: on the night of the fire twelve years ago, Zhou Dalang went to the door of West Warehouse Three, held a tally register in his hand, and said, ‘I’m going to lift the mat.’ This is the testimony of the person who received the jar, given from across the awning; after first refuting the right hand and then identifying the left little finger, the testimony and evidence may be relied upon.”
“Two accounts not to be settled, recorded as pending collection—”
“First: who set the fire. This man only delivered the jar to the door; he says he left as soon as he had done so. I believe half of what he says. As for who set the fire, that requires another mouth, another ledger.”
“Second: whether Zhou Dalang lifted that mat. He said he would lift it; saying it does not mean he lifted it. Lifting it does not mean he saw clearly. Seeing clearly does not mean he died in the fire. The line I myself most want—I myself hold it down and forbid myself to enter it.”
When she had finished writing, she set the charcoal stub down, pressed both hands onto that torn cloth, and held them there for a long time.
Only one thought kept turning in her mind, turning until her palms went cold: that moment when he lifted the mat—that was the reason for those two jars of shaodaozi he had put on credit at my counter over those three days. It was not he who put them on credit; it was Qijin who put them on credit for him, in the same ledger, on the same date. Someone had long since written out the way he was to die for him: a cargo escort who had bought strong liquor, entered the warehouse at night, and carelessly caused an accident at the stove.
A warehouse of salt had been emptied, the ledger had “empty” written in it, one fire burned the ledger, and then they added in a man who was going to lift the mat.
She raised her head. Her eyes were red and swollen, but her face had already been wiped clean—that was the face she wore behind the counter when she had balanced a dead account.
She folded the strip of cloth into four, tucked it close against her body, together with that rubbing.
Then she got up, dragged the dry-ration bag out from the corner, divided it into two portions, each with one coarse bowl and one bowl of water. She first placed the portion for the east end three feet outside the awning door, pushed it in with the tip of her foot, without showing herself, without uttering a word. Turning back, she brought the other portion to the west-end room where Han Qijin was—when she got to the door, she suddenly stopped, untied the grass-rope knot on his wrist, tied it again with a finger’s width of slack, and looped it back around the back of his own hand.
From beginning to end, she did not make a sound.
Only after retreating to the middle room did she lean close to Lu Wenfeng’s ear, keeping all her breath pressed behind her teeth, her voice so low that the slightest sound of pond water would cover it:
“I won’t touch the entry about ‘setting the fire’—you were right. If I touch it, then I’m no longer settling accounts; I’m seeking revenge.”
“But that little booklet.” Her knuckle tapped the stool board very lightly. “Brother Zhou escorted cargo for eleven years; his tally register never left his body. He kept numbers even more rigidly than I kept vegetable prices. Fire burns paper—but does it burn a copper tally tube? That copper tally tube at his waist—twelve years ago, I didn’t see his face, and I didn’t see his belongings either. Gu Changting gave me twenty taels, but he didn’t even return a single copper tally tube to me.”
She paused. The bit of fire in her eyes sank back down, burning very steadily.
“I’m marking this account as ‘pending collection.’ The place to collect it is at the county office: relics from the fire scene should have been taken under official seal. Gu Changting rose three ranks. He dared burn ledgers, but he may not have dared burn a cargo escort’s waist token—that was an item of the Grain Transport Guild, something the Grain Transport Guild would come to claim.”
She straightened her back and pressed the bamboo hat down onto her head.
“Tonight there are three rooms. I’ll keep watch in the middle. You sleep the first half of the night; I’ll switch with you for the second half—don’t argue. This is the rule in my shop: the shopkeeper is the last one to put out the lamp.”
After a pause, her voice was so low it was almost inaudible:
“The face-to-face record will be tomorrow. The character ‘feng’ is still not to be written.”
“...But tonight I learned one thing: my Brother Zhou did not go there to put out the fire, and he did not go there to die. He went there to count hemp sacks.”
She wiped her face and smiled once, a very faint smile.
“In this life, that is the one kind of person I truly respect.”

Lu Wenfeng holds back the phrase “settle it as a dead account”: “Record the testimony first; don’t settle it as a dead account. A partitioned awning can prevent collusion, but it can’t make him tell the truth.”
He says in a low voice toward the east room: “Where did you go after leaving West Third Warehouse, and how long after did you see the fire? Could you see the face of the person carrying the lantern clearly? What pattern was on the copper tally tube at his waist? Answer one by one, and don’t guess on our behalf.”

What Liu Sanniang did first was take the charcoal stub and revise the piece of cloth on her knees.
Over the words she had just written—“one death entry posted”—she blackened them out stroke by stroke, rubbing until the rag grew fuzzy. Beside them she wrote four new characters:
“Confession pending comparison.”
After writing them, she raised her eyes and looked at Lu Wenfeng for one breath, then added another line:
“I was too hasty. Keeping them separated by awnings can prevent collusion, but it cannot prevent him from filling my gaps with words he has overheard. I take this entry back.”
Then she suddenly turned the cloth over, pressed it on her knees, and hunched her back to block the light leaking through the reed curtain. The charcoal stub flew through several strokes—once she finished, she immediately folded it into a small square, stuffed it into Lu Wenfeng’s palm, and pressed her fingers hard twice on the back of his hand.
Taking another corner of cloth, she wrote for him to see:
“Inside this is what I want. Hold it first; you don’t have to look. Wait until he finishes describing the pattern on the tally tube, then open it—if it matches, it matches; if it doesn’t, it doesn’t. If I say it first, it becomes me teaching him.”
Her knuckles tapped once on the bench, very lightly.
“My account—I will seal my own mouth first.”
The strip of cloth was handed out. The boatman took it and squatted outside the awning door of the east room, reading from it in a flat voice, as if counting hemp sacks:
“After you left the warehouse gate, where did you go. How long before you saw the fire. Did you see clearly the face of the man carrying the lantern. The copper tally tube at his waist—what pattern did it have. Answer one by one. No guessing.”
Inside the awning, the mat rustled for a while.
“...I went along the foot of the wall and out the firewood gate. There was a small boat waiting at the river wharf. I didn’t know the boatman; he didn’t say a word.” The man’s voice was so hoarse it rasped. “The boat went downstream, passed two sluice gates. At the second bend I looked back—and saw red. How long? More than one quarter-hour, less than two.”
Liu Sanniang’s fingers tightened on her knees.
“The fire didn’t start by the kitchen.” The man suddenly added this on his own, his voice trembling. “I’ve escorted night goods plenty of times; I know where the inn’s kitchen is—the fire shot up from the roof of the west-end warehouse, and in an instant half the sky was red. It burned too fast. It didn’t look like firewood—it looked like something had been poured.”
The boatman read the third item.
“I didn’t see the face clearly. The lantern was in his own hand, shining on the ledger, not his face; his back was to the light, and I was in the dark. I only remember he wasn’t tall, the ledger was tucked in the crook of his left arm, and his right hand held the lantern.”
The fourth item.
Inside the awning, there was one breath of silence.
“The tally tube... around the waist of the tube there was a fine copper wire band. It went around three times. The wire end was twisted into a little knot—not a dead knot, the kind where it’s twisted back and fastened. There was also a dent on the tube’s cap, like it had been struck.”
In the thatched hut, only the pond water could be heard slapping the wooden stakes.
Liu Sanniang folded down without making a sound, her forehead pressed against the rag on her knees, her shoulders jerking again and again. Her teeth bit into the old ring of teeth marks on the back of her own hand—biting down, not letting out a single sound.
Three turns. The wire end twisted back and fastened.
That was a return clasp. A method for tying cargo on the grain-transport routes, one she had learned at the ferry crossing; the one who taught her was Brother Zhou. Eleven years ago, his copper tally tube had split, and he could not bear to replace it. Behind the counter of Banhuchun, she had used the copper wire for stringing account books to band it for him three times, twisting a return clasp, and had even laughed at him: “Brother Zhou, this tally tube of yours will live longer than you.”
Lu Wenfeng opened the little square of cloth in his palm. On it was her writing, the charcoal pressed until it shone:
“One fine copper wire around the waist of the tube, three turns, wire end in a return clasp. One struck dent on the cap. This wire was banded by my own hands, eleven years ago, behind my counter.”
She raised her head. Her face was a mess, blood marks seeping from the back of her hand, but she had already sat up straight.
The charcoal stub fell onto the cloth, stroke by stroke, slow as if tracing characters:
“Record: the two sides accord; the seal came first, the confession after. This is evidence.”
“Still do not enter it as a death account. The object must be matched—the copper tally tube, if it is among the fire-scene relics officially sealed by the county, will show at one glance the three turns of copper wire, the return clasp, and the struck dent on the cap. This object belongs to the transport gang; the transport gang can demand it. I cannot demand it as the shopkeeper of Banhuchun; I can demand it as Zhou Dalang’s sworn younger sister.”
She paused, then added another stroke. The force of the stroke suddenly grew heavy:
“Also record one item to be obtained—the largest item: the oil account.”
She raised her eyes. Beneath the red threads in them, what burned was the light of abacus beads.
“Master Lu. Two jars of Shaodaozi liquor, thirty-odd jin—enough to soak one door plank wet, not enough to set a warehouse roof on fire. He said the fire shot up from the west-end warehouse roof, turned half the sky red in an instant, as if something had been poured—that was oil. To burn through a warehouse stacked to the beams with husks, it would take several piculs of tung oil, several piculs of lamp oil; someone would have had to push carts into the depot, weigh them, and enter them in the accounts. Oil coming into the depot had to pass through the hands of the accounts office.”
She brought the charcoal stub down on the cloth, making a black pit.
“Shen Henian was the accounts office.”
“Those two jars of Shaodaozi were a front put out for people to see. The oil that truly burned the goods depot was written in the depot’s income ledger—that ledger, Gu Changting may dare to burn, but incoming goods at the depot have to be reported to the likin checkpoint, and the checkpoint has duplicate registers. The likin checkpoint’s registers are in official hands, not in his house.”
She took a deep breath, folded that piece of cloth into quarters, and tucked it against her body, stacking it together with the rubbing and the white cloth strip. Her hand pressed it firmly against her chest.
Then she stood up.
She made no sound. She only extended three fingers, pointing first to the east room, then to the west room, and finally to the bench where she herself had been sitting—separate custody, no passing messages, she would guard the middle. Then she pressed two fingers together downward, and swept them horizontally toward the water: the boat was to lie crosswise, the oar not to be put away, no lamp to be lit.
After giving the instructions, she leaned to Lu Wenfeng’s ear, her breath pressed behind her teeth:
“You sleep the first half of the night. I’ll wake you for the second half—don’t argue. In this shop of mine, the shopkeeper is the last one to put out the lamp.”
After a pause, her voice was so low it almost scattered into the pond water:
“The three bowls of noodles go on tomorrow’s account. The character ‘by order’ is not to be written.”
She wiped her face, pressed the bamboo hat down over her head to her brow bone, and suddenly gave a very faint laugh.
“...Those three turns of copper wire of mine kept a letter for him for eleven years.”
“Tonight, someone spoke this confession for him. Brother Zhou, that tally tube of yours truly did live longer than you.”
